title: Start Customizing NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano with Prime Intellect Lab in Minutes | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA walks through customizing Nemotron 3 Nano (nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-BF16) on Prime Intellect Lab's hosted RL service, lifting accuracy on a 32-problem math-python held-out set from 21.9% to 90.6% via a 100-step LoRA RLVR run costing under $5. The piece doubles as a positioning argument: open weights plus data plus recipes, plus third-party hosted training on NVIDIA Blackwell, mean a small adapted model can substitute for a more expensive broadly capable one.

themes.theme: Measured RLVR lift on Nemotron 3 Nano

insights.claim: A 100-step LoRA reinforcement-learning run on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano raised accuracy on 32 held-out math problems from 21.9% (7/32) to 90.6% (29/32), an absolute gain of 68.75 percentage points.
insights.speaker: Chris Alexiuk
insights.so_what: A ~69-point task lift from a sub-$5 run is the strongest available argument that task-specific small-model adaptation undercuts frontier-model API spend.
insights.quote: accuracy increased from 21.9% (7/32) to 90.6% (29/32), an absolute increase of 68.75 percentage points

insights.claim: The entire Nemotron 3 Nano customization run, including hosted rollouts, 100 training steps, and inference, cost less than $5 in total spend on Prime Intellect Lab.
insights.speaker: Chris Alexiuk
insights.so_what: If meaningful domain adaptation genuinely costs single-digit dollars, the marginal buyer of frontier inference tokens has a cheap escape hatch, a structural headwind for per-token API pricing.
insights.quote: Nemotron 3 Nano got better at this task with a total spend of less than $5.

insights.claim: Reward statistics on the Python-math task show variance collapsing alongside the accuracy gain: average reward moved from 0.219 with std 0.413 at baseline to 0.906 with std 0.291 after training on an identical evaluation configuration.
insights.speaker: Chris Alexiuk
insights.so_what: Falling reward variance alongside a rising mean indicates the model learned the tool-use protocol rather than getting lucky, a cleaner signal than headline accuracy alone.
insights.locator: Your results should contain the following

insights.claim: Of the 24 prompts whose outcome changed between the baseline and the trained Nemotron 3 Nano adapter, 23 improved and only one regressed, indicating near-monotonic gains rather than a redistribution of errors.
insights.speaker: Chris Alexiuk
insights.so_what: A 23:1 improve-to-regress ratio is the kind of evidence that makes small-model adaptation defensible in production, not just in benchmarks.
insights.quote: Of the 24 prompts that had different outcomes between baseline and final, 23 improved, and one regressed.

insights.claim: The baseline Nemotron 3 Nano failure mode was procedural rather than mathematical: the model exhausted its five-turn cap calling unsupported tools and returned an empty response instead of a boxed answer.
insights.speaker: Chris Alexiuk
insights.so_what: If small-model deficits are agentic-protocol failures rather than reasoning failures, cheap RL fixes them, compressing the perceived capability gap versus frontier models.
insights.quote: the model fails to produce a boxed response because it exhausted five turns calling unsupported tools
insights.locator: This is an example of a failing prompt for our baseline model

insights.claim: The published Nemotron 3 Nano RL config uses max_steps=100, batch_size=32, rollouts_per_example=8, learning_rate=2e-5 and lora_alpha=16, with sampling at max_tokens=2048, temperature=1.0 and thinking disabled.
insights.speaker: Chris Alexiuk
insights.so_what: A fully specified, reproducible hyperparameter set turns a vendor demo into something a buyer can replicate and price out internally.

insights.claim: Sampling eight attempts per selected task gives the trainer a comparative signal inside each rollout group, with four such groups forming a batch of 32; the group-relative structure is what supplies learning signal in this RLVR setup.
insights.speaker: Chris Alexiuk
insights.so_what: Group-relative rollout sampling is the dominant post-training pattern and explains why RL post-training consumes far more inference compute than training compute.
insights.quote: The trainer samples eight attempts for each selected task, giving it a comparative signal inside each rollout group.
insights.locator: This config outlines how we want to train our model

insights.claim: The math-python environment defaults to 100 turns but the tutorial caps each rollout at five assistant turns specifically to penalize the model for repeatedly calling tools without producing a final response.
insights.speaker: Chris Alexiuk
insights.so_what: Turn caps as a reward-shaping lever show how cheaply agentic behavior can be tuned, relevant to anyone modelling per-query token consumption in agent products.
insights.quote: This penalizes the model heavily for repeatedly calling tools without producing a final response.
insights.locator: NOTE: The environment has a default of 100 turns

insights.claim: Reward in this reinforcement-learning-with-verifiable-rewards setup is strictly binary, 1 for a correct response and 0 for incorrect or missing, meaning the entire gain came from verifiable outcome rewards with no learned reward model.
insights.speaker: Chris Alexiuk
insights.so_what: Verifiable rewards remove reward-model training cost and its failure modes, which is why RLVR is spreading faster than preference-based RL in production stacks.
insights.quote: The reward is binary: 1 means the model produced a correct response, and 0 means the model produced an incorrect or missing response.
insights.locator: Figure 1 is an example of our reward distribution

insights.claim: Experimental discipline matters more than scale in hosted RL: if every rollout attempt receives the same score the trainer has little signal to work with, so practitioners should inspect high-, middle- and low-reward rollouts and watch token use and truncation.
insights.speaker: Chris Alexiuk
insights.so_what: Reward collapse being the primary failure mode tells you where hosted-RL platforms will differentiate: diagnostics, not raw GPU throughput.
insights.quote: If every attempt receives the same score, the trainer has little signal to work with.
insights.locator: When experimenting, begin with small variations

insights.claim: The NVIDIA Nemotron 3 family spans three published tiers with concrete hosted identifiers: Nano at NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-BF16, Super at NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B-BF16, and Ultra at NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B-NVFP4.
insights.speaker: Chris Alexiuk
insights.so_what: A 30B/120B/550B open-weight ladder with NVFP4 at the top tier signals NVIDIA is seeding demand for its own low-precision formats through free model weights.

insights.claim: Prime Intellect offers hosted reinforcement learning on Nemotron 3 Ultra running on NVIDIA Blackwell infrastructure, making the largest open Nemotron tier trainable without owning a GPU cluster.
insights.speaker: Chris Alexiuk
insights.so_what: A neocloud selling managed Blackwell RL on NVIDIA's own open models is a datapoint on how NVIDIA converts free weights into rented silicon demand.
insights.quote: Nemotron 3 Ultra is the high-capacity option in the family, and Prime Intellect has support for hosted reinforcement learning on NVIDIA Blackwell infrastructure.

insights.claim: Scaling from Nemotron 3 Nano to Super or Ultra requires changing only the model identifier line in the config, with the identical workflow, environment, and CLI commands otherwise unchanged.
insights.speaker: Chris Alexiuk
insights.so_what: Zero-friction scale-up between model tiers is how hosted platforms convert cheap experiments into large paid training runs; watch the conversion rate, not the free tier.
insights.locator: Training larger models with Prime Intellect Lab

insights.claim: Prime Intellect Lab handles hosted rollout, training, and inference infrastructure so the practitioner needs no local GPU cluster, with local setup taking about five minutes and the full loop 5-15 minutes.
insights.speaker: Chris Alexiuk
insights.so_what: Training-as-a-service collapsing setup to minutes expands the pool of teams doing custom post-training, growing aggregate GPU demand beyond the hyperscalers.
insights.quote: Prime Intellect handles the hosted rollout, training, and inference infrastructure; you don’t need to manage a local GPU cluster.

insights.claim: The Nemotron customization workflow pins exact versions throughout (prime==0.6.17, Python 3.13, math_python at 0.1.10) while warning that model availability and pricing change over time so the live CLI catalog is the source of truth.
insights.speaker: Chris Alexiuk
insights.so_what: An explicit caveat that hosted-training prices move frequently is a reminder that neocloud RL pricing is not yet stable enough to underwrite long-term cost models.
insights.quote: Treat the live CLI catalog as the source of truth rather than copying an identifier or price from a static article.
insights.locator: Note: Model availability and pricing change over time

insights.claim: NVIDIA argues that without customization buyers may overpay for a more broadly capable model when a lower-cost model could be adapted to the specific task needed.
insights.speaker: Chris Alexiuk
insights.so_what: This is NVIDIA explicitly arguing against paying frontier-model prices, a competitive framing aimed at closed-model API vendors while preserving NVIDIA silicon demand either way.
insights.quote: we may overpay for a more broadly capable model when a lower-cost model could be adapted to the task we need

insights.claim: NVIDIA positions open weights as insufficient on their own, arguing data, evaluation code, and training recipes determine what a user can understand, reproduce, and deploy, and publishes Nemotron 3 with all of them.
insights.speaker: Chris Alexiuk
insights.so_what: Raising the bar for what counts as open is a competitive attack on open-weight rivals shipping weights only, and makes Nemotron stickier for enterprises needing auditability.
insights.quote: Open weights are an important part of the equation, but they aren’t the entire equation.

insights.claim: The article's stated core value in open models is not free weights or managed infrastructure but that the entire improvement loop can be inspected and repeated, framing reproducibility as the durable advantage.
insights.speaker: Chris Alexiuk
insights.so_what: If reproducibility is the differentiator, the winners in open models are those publishing recipes and environments, not just the largest checkpoint.
insights.quote: It’s that the entire improvement loop can be inspected and repeated.

insights.claim: Deploying a trained LoRA adapter on Prime Intellect creates a billable inference endpoint whose state moves NOT_DEPLOYED to DEPLOYING to DEPLOYED, and the article instructs users to delete it as cleanup.
insights.speaker: Chris Alexiuk
insights.so_what: Per-endpoint billing on idle adapters is the monetization hook in hosted-training platforms: cheap to train, metered to serve.
insights.quote: Deployment creates a billable inference endpoint.
